utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case IT-03-69-T. The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I think that last Friday we adjourned in closed session which should not have been done in closed session. We should have gone into open session and then adjourned until today in open session. I apologise for that mistake. Mr. Groome or Mr. Farr, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the Prosecution calls Radislav Maksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Farr, looking back I see that in 2007 the witness is scheduled for one hour in chief and then suddenly he is 2 and a half hours, and now I do understand he's reduced to 2 hours. Nevertheless, of course, the Chamber wonders why one hour was good enough in 2007 and why we need now two hours

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment I'm not familiar with the details of that history, but I'll certainly go as quickly as I can and I expect to finish within two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. I didn't verify with you but no protective measures as far as I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Maksic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, before you give evidence, Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration. The text of it is handed out to you now by the usher. I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Our screens are not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your screens are not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The one in the centre is so as far as I'm concerned we can continue, but this screen in front of me isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you have logged in in a way --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In the usual way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if you log out and try to do it again sometimes that helps, because I was informed that there had been some problems with our screens as well. If it is not resolved, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll receive assistance anyhow, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Maksic, you'll be first examined by Mr. Farr. Mr. Farr is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Maksic. Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, I can hear you clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Radislav Maksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, I'm going to first ask you a number of questions relating to your prior testimony in the Martic case. Did you testify in the Martic case on 6 and 7 February, 2006?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Have you recently had the chance to review audio recordings of your testimony in the Martic case in your own language?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Page 1194 of the English transcript of your Martic testimony contains the following statement: "I heard that there were paramilitary units involved in the attack on Pakrac. Arkan's Men, Giska's Men, Captain Dragan's Men, and some others whose names I don't know." Did you have a correction to the location "Pakrac"?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Instead of Pakrac, it should read Gospic. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: With that correction, do the recordings of your testimony accurately reflect the evidence you gave in that case?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And taking that correction into account, if you were asked the same questions here today that you were asked during your Martic testimony, would you give the same answers in substance?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: In substance, yes, they would be the same. I wouldn't change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of that prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders the witness's prior testimony in the Martic case on 6 and 7 February, 2006, as a Prosecution exhibit. A consolidated transcript of both days of testimony has been uploaded in e-court as 65 ter number 5749.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P951, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll now turn to the 92 ter related exhibits for this witness's Martic testimony. Before court I handed out an updated list of these Exhibits to the Defence and the Court Officer. There are 16 related exhibits, 15 of these were admitted during this witness's testimony in Martic, one was marked for identification. We seek the same treatment of the exhibits in this case at this time. The 15 documents that we seek to have admitted bear the following 65 ter numbers: 3890, 1086, 1081, 4630, 3896, 1094, 1095, 2818, 1587, 3967, 3923, 1590, 1903, 393, and 3926. The document that we seek to have marked for identification is 65 ter number 3940.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to invite Madam Registrar to reserve or to prepare the exhibit numbers to be assigned to these documents. And the one marked for identification, Mr. Farr, is?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: 3940, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is -- you are not seeking admission yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please give us the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought that it was the 3940 which was to be MFI'd, or did I --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's the -- no, you are correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then 3926 would --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: We would move to have that admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Then 3940 will be P967 MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first see whether there's any objections. If there are not, P952, is that the first one, the transcript is incomplete. Mr. Farr, was that 65 ter 3809, Madam Registrar, was --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's 3890 in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that has received number P952. P952 up to and including P966 are admitted into evidence. P967 is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, now that your prior testimony has been admitted into evidence, I will read a summary of your prior testimony for the benefit of the public. The witness is a retired JNA officer who held various positions in the Belgrade Corps and retired with the rank of colonel. In late September 1991, the witness was transferred to Knin along with three other JNA officers to organise the staff of the SAO Krajina TO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel please read slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters. To organise the staff of the SAO Krajina TO which did not exist as an institution prior to that time. The witness testified that while he was in the SAO Krajina, the SAO Krajina TO staff was understaffed, ill-equipped, and lacking the financial resources to establish units of the Territorial Defence. In addition, the JNA and the SAO Krajina police had first priority for the most able recruits which made it difficult to establish TO units. While the SAO Krajina TO units were in theory subordinated to the staff of the SAO Krajina TO, in reality they were subordinated to JNA units in the area. The term "marticevci" was used to refer to all forces of the Ministry of the Interior or MUP of the SAO Krajina. According to the witness, as Babic was president of the SAO Krajina, in theory, he had authority over all other government employees and organisations including Martic and his Ministry of the Interior. In reality, however, Babic exerted little or no control or influence over the work of the SAO Krajina MUP. The witness testified that Martic attended meetings with the commander of the JNA 9th corps. With Martic's permission, the Krajina police participated in joint operations with the JNA. The witness also described the relations between the SAO Krajina TO staff and the Ministry of Defence of Serbia and testified that the SAO Krajina TO staff was totally dependent on the support of the Ministry of Defence of Serbia in terms of personnel, financing, and logistics. The witness stated that the Ministry of the Interior of Krajina had logistical support from the Republic of Serbia MUP and that this included equipment with which Martic had established an excellent communication system, including long-range radio stations. The witness discussed the relationship between Martic and Babic noting that they did not get along and could in fact never agree on anything. The witness believes that Babic established the SAO Krajina TO staff to counter the influence of Martic. The witness identified Jovica Stanisic and someone with the nickname Frenki as members of the state security service. During his time in the Krajina, the witness saw Martic and Frenki and the same group of people on several occasions in Knin and Korenica. He also saw Stanisic on two or three occasions during his time in the Krajina. The witness also testified that Vojislav Seselj visited the Krajina on at least one occasion. The witness further testified that volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were incorporated into the units of the JNA 9th Corps and that they received all of their orders through the usual military chain of command. In December 1991, Milan Babic appointed the witness to the position of commander of the SAO Krajina TO replacing Ilija Djujic. As Babic did not have legal grounds to make this appointment, however, the appointment had no legal force. Indeed at the witness's request, Babic's order was annulled in late December 1991 by the General Staff of the SFRY armed forces, and the witness subsequently returned to Belgrade. This concludes the summary of the witness's prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Farr. We still have problems with the transcript. We also have problems now. I do understand that the system will be restarted and hopefully then it works again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, I would now like to ask you a number of questions to clarify and expand on your prior testimony which has been admitted into evidence. To begin with at page 1135 of your Martic testimony, you indicated that in 1991 you held a position in the staff of the Belgrade Corps. My question is, did the staff of the Belgrade Corps have control over or responsibility for any military equipment and weaponry at this time?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Can you repeat the question in terms of what military equipment are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did the Belgrade -- the staff of the Belgrade Corps have responsibility for any warehouses or storehouses containing military equipment or weaponry?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Belgrade Corps had a large warehouse which was used as a storage facility by other units as well. However, they were given support to by the Belgrade Corps in the place called Bubanj Potok in the immediate vicinity of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did the staff of the Belgrade Corps at any time receive orders to provide equipment or weaponry to anyone?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: We received orders from the General Staff, that's to say from the technical administration. We received orders that certain individuals should be issued with certain elements of equipment and weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And who were those certain individuals that you were ordered to provide equipment and weaponry?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: They were for the most part leaders of volunteers or those who organised volunteer units, and they were predominantly organised by parties, mainly by the Serbian Radical Party and Vuk Draskovic's party, the Serbian Renewal Movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And did the Belgrade Corps in fact provide weapons to these volunteers provided by the Serbian Radical Party and Vuk Draskovic's party?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, the Belgrade Corps, or rather its commander through his staff, merely complied with the orders of the superior command and issued a certain quantity of weapons as requested by representatives of the these parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Maksic, in 1991 were you acquainted with General Andrija Biorcevic of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew him from earlier on and I knew him in 1991. He was the commander of the Novi Sad Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see General Biorcevic at a training-ground in the vicinity of Bogojevo at some point in 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, the training-ground is called Erdut and I saw him, yes, or rather, I met with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And can you please describe this occasion when you saw General Biorcevic on this training-ground?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I received a task -- or rather, I can testify about the period between the 1st of October and the end of December 1991. As for the various dates and months, well, I don't remember those but I do remember events. One scouts company, reconnaissance company, was subordinated to the commander of the Novi Sad Corps. I took the company along to Erdut in order to resubordinate it. I was supposed to receive an order from Biorcevic to the effect that the unit should become part of the Novi Sad Corps, and that's how we met and discussed the various events happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation -- sorry. Did you have a conversation regarding the arming of any particular group with General Biorcevic at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes. Did you have a conversation at that time with General Biorcevic regarding the arming of any particular group?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Our apologies, we are not fully staffed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'll repeats the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir on this occasion -- we still have B/C/S on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We now hear English on channel 4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear English now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now can hear English. Mr. Farr, let's give it a try. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, this occasion you've just been describing when you saw General Biorcevic, did you have a conversation with him about the arming of any particular group?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: While I was there, I saw some soldiers one day who were armed with automatic weapons that were not part of the standard issue of JNA. I asked him who are these guys and he said they are Arkan's Men. Then I asked, well, where do they get these weapons from, and he said, you know what, you're asking too much, little man, because the JNA did not have -- did not possess those kinds of weapons, only weapons for fighting close combat, that's what the JNA had.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did -- did General Biorcevic say anything on that occasion that allowed you to surmise where those men had obtained those weapons?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the weapons that was the case then, and I suppose it still is, can only be had by those who had authority -- who were empowered by law to have weapons; in other words, the army and the police. If the weapons did not belong to the army, and I'm just guessing now, then that must mean that either Arkan bought it and then smuggled it or that he obtained it from the police, but that is only my conjecture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not want to interfere with the witness because he mentions a little earlier how many people he saw there, how many men, and that did not enter the transcript, so if we could just -- if he can just specify, he was referring to those fighters who had the special weapons, so if Mr. Farr could ask the question again or just ask him to confirm this, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, apparently we're seeking the number of people who had such arms. Could you tell us how many you saw which possessed these arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I met three to four such men. I did not mention numbers. I asked about Arkan's Men. I asked him who were Arkan's Men. I didn't ask any -- I didn't put any further questions. I didn't ask about the units or its composition or the manpower levels because that was not within my competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And can you tell us more specifically where you saw these three to four men, was it indoors, was it outdoors, was it in a building?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: It was outdoors. It was actually outside of the training-ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. I'd now like to ask you about your arrival in the Krajina. At page 1135 of your Martic testimony you stated: "In late September 1991, I went to Krajina as chief of the operations department of the Krajina TO staff." My question is, can you tell me how you travelled to the Krajina, in other words, what was your route and what means of transportation did you use?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: From Belgrade to Bihac I travelled by air, from Bihac to Korenica by car, and from Korenica to Knin by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And were you travelling with anyone else during this journey?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: We were taken there, our guide as it were was General Kuzmanovic, I'm not sure that that was his actual name, but I believe so. He was assistant minister of defence in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you stop in the course of this journey for any reason?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: We stopped in Bihac, we had to wait for transportation for about three to four hours. And then Kuzmanovic went, he just disappeared, and I only saw him again in the evening, later in the evening in Korenica at the hotel when the driver came to pick us up and take us to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: When you first arrived in Knin, where were you accommodated?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: When we first arrived in Knin, we were accommodated in the barracks. We shared the room, the dorm with some 20 soldiers or so, and there were a couple of officers in addition to myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in that barracks?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I believe we remained there about two to three days because it was impossible to find suitable accommodation either for the three to four of us who arrived there, nor did we have premises for our staff. Or rather, we left, we went away -- we went there although no preparations had been made for them to actually accept us there, so there were no working conditions whatsoever for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And after these two to three days in the barrack, where were you accommodated after that?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: After that they actually freed two rooms in a hotel of sorts. I can't recall the name of the hotel, but they actually referred to it as an old people's home because that's what it used to be in the past and that's what they still used for the hotel. So that's where we were accommodated. We had -- we slept there and we had our meals there. As for work, we were accommodated in four offices of the Municipal Assembly of Knin and we took up, as it were, our positions there as the staff. We just were accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You've just told us that your offices were in the Municipal Assembly building. Can you tell us where the headquarters of the Ministry of the Interior or MUP of the SAO Krajina were?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: That was nearby. Knin is a small town, you can cross from one end to the other on foot in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And can you tell us where the staff of the TO of Knin municipality was located?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: The staff of the TO of Knin municipality was in some buildings that were on the Knin hill where the fort was, and that's where the Territorial Defence staff of Knin was. And some 10 to 15 days later, I believe they moved out of those premises at the Knin fort.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the commander of the staff of the TO of Knin municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I remember that this man because of his age had to retire, or was about to retire, so that we actually took him over at the TO staff as a finance officer. I can tell you the name but I don't know if I should. Oh, well, I have it written down somewhere. I'll try to call it up. Radulovic, that's what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I would now like to ask you some questions about Dragan Vasiljkovic. Had you heard of Dragan Vasiljkovic prior to your arrival in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I had heard of Dragan Vasiljkovic before I went to Krajina, or rather, I knew him as Captain Dragan. I didn't know his name. You could read about him in the press and you could also see him on Belgrade TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And following your arrival in the Krajina, did you have any conversations with anyone about Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you ever learn where Captain Dragan and his men had been accommodated prior to your arrival in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, when I arrived in Krajina, Captain Dragan was no longer there, but the TO staff, the Knin TO staff commander, told me that Captain Dragan had used some of the buildings on the Knin fort and also some premises in Golubic, which was a camp or perhaps a training-ground, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And I think you may have already answered this, but do you know whether Captain Dragan and his men were still accommodated at the Knin fortress when you arrived in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you ever personally see Captain Dragan during your time in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I met Captain Dragan sometime in October or November, I can't really remember. When I arrived one evening at the hotel to stay the night there was a room, a conference room of some sort. I saw a person in uniform, but I wouldn't really pay attention to this because there were many people in uniform who milled around in the hotel because there was a big restaurant in the hotel where they came to have their meals. So I wouldn't have paid any attention had I not seen a combat vehicle outside the hotel, a BOV vehicle. I asked whose vehicle that was and I was told it was Captain Dragan's and this is the occasion when we met. I asked him, well, man, why are you going around in a combat vehicle and then parking it here. Just remove it from there. And he said that he had been given this vehicle from -- by Mr. Martic and that he could use it. And then I called him and asked him to remove that vehicle that was outside the hotel so that the civilians who were there wouldn't wonder what this was about. And then jokingly I said, well, if you don't remove it in two hours, I will, although I had no resources to do that. But two hours later, neither the vehicle nor Captain Dragan were there any more and I have never seen him since.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You just said, "and then I called him and asked him to remove that vehicle that was outside the hotel." Who did you call?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I called the duty officer of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And why did you call the duty officer of the Ministry of the Interior in particular?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, because the police was responsible for law and order and they were the ones who provided security for various buildings and so on and so forth. That was not something that was within the army's competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you about a meeting that you were invited to attend shortly after you arrived in the Krajina. At page 1179 of your Martic testimony you said the following: "We should distinguish between the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia and the state security service. These are two different institutions. Several days after my arrival in Knin, I was invited to attend a meeting. Djujic, Kasim, and I were invited. Mr. Martic was present as well as was Mr. Frenki, whom I didn't know. The name didn't mean anything to me, and I simply wasn't interested in the person." My question is, how did you learn that this person was called Frenki?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really learn. Someone mentioned it, one of the members of the group. Someone told me Frenki is present as well, and then I asked him, well, what Frenki, what does that mean, what are you talking about because I had never seen the man or met him or even heard of him, because the state security service was not something that I had anything to do with, nor was I interested in their work or their organisation and so on. Although, of course, through school you do learn about this service, and I did have an idea what their job was, but I had no official contacts. There was no reason for me to work with them because there was also a military security service and the information was provided by this service for us within the military so that we had nothing to do with the state security service, no connections, no contacts of any sort. So that I don't know, I sort of just said, so what, why are you telling me this that there's this Frenki there, and who is he anyway. And we did not talk about him anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you recall who it was who told you who Frenki was?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, there were five or six of us, we were waiting outside the office, waiting for the meeting to start, and I can't really recall as I sit here who exactly of the group told me about it. But then the Chief of Staff of the TO staff, General Djujic, and then Kasim, and I was the chief of the operation staff, we -- they said that we weren't -- that Colonel Kasim and I were not required to be at the meeting and that we can go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You said that you were waiting outside the office for the meeting to start. Where was this office located, in what place or building?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: It was at the fort. When I say in the fort, I've already explained there was a hill near Knin. This was probably an old fortification, such towns are numerous in that part of the world, and then there were various buildings built up there on that same hill. I don't know what they were used for, but I know that the TO staff of Krajina was housed there, or I apologise, the Knin TO staff was housed there. I know because when I arrived, I went to the staff premises to meet the commander and to be briefed by him on the situation and what was going on there and so on, because we didn't really know much about what was going on there and we did not receive any information on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you. And again you may have already answered this, but did you learn which institution or organisation Mr. Frenki worked for?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: No. I knew about Mr. Simatovic, I didn't even know his first name, I only learned it later. All I know about him is what I've already mentioned here. I don't know who he is or what he was, nor was I interested in that. I could have found out had I wanted to, but I didn't. I didn't know what organisation he belonged to or what he did for them. Because Mr. Simatovic did not have any influence over the TO staff. He could not exert any influence over them, and I was looking for men who could exert some influence because we needed assistance in terms of information, communications, organisation and so on. So that's all I knew about Mr. Simatovic because he had nothing to do with any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you ever learn what the subject matter of this meeting was to be?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: No. We asked our commander, or rather, the TO Krajina staff commander General Djujic what was going on and what the meeting was about and whether there was any role for us there. He didn't say anything, he just said there was nothing for you to do here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You've just described one occasion in which you saw this person who was identified to you as Frenki. Can you estimate how many times in total you saw the person who was identified to you as Frenki while you were in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I saw him twice. On that occasion at the fort and once in Korenica and since then I've never seen or heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Still at page 1179 of your Martic testimony, you went on to say: "On another occasion, Stanisic was present as well. This didn't mean much to me because I was not familiar with the police and security services. I met Stanisic maybe just once or twice prior to that in a meeting." At page 1180 when you were asked for his first name, you said it was Jovica and went on to say: "At the time he was either deputy or chief of the state security service." My question is, how did you learn that Stanisic was then either deputy chief or chief of the state security service?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't know that at the time. I only learned it later on. What I said about Mr. Simatovic, well, the same would apply for Mr. Stanisic. In 1991 at some point I read, maybe on the internet or some place else, that Mr. Stanisic was -- had been appointed as the chief of the state security service in 1991, which again didn't mean anything to me personally because I had no official contacts with the state security service, nor was I in any way involved in their work. They didn't interest me just as I was not of any interest to them either.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate how many times you saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to -- I hope this isn't improper, but to refer Your Honours to page 1184 of the same transcript. I think it would have been given a clearer context to the witness's answer in that trial. At line 2 when the witness said in relation to who was the head of state security, that he didn't know who he was at the end of 1991. Who it was at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, do you feel assisted by this or rather the opposite?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Jordash is correct. That perhaps might have provided better context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it was appropriate to do it, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently, Mr. Farr feels to be assisted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, are you able to estimate how many times you saw Mr. Stanisic during your time in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I saw him once or twice. Well, for sure twice. I saw him once in Korenica as I did Mr. Simatovic, and once I saw him in Knin. And I wasn't really wondering about why he was there because many eminent personnel had visited Knin at the time and it was normal that I should see him there as the chief of the state security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: However, I didn't give either Stanisic or Simatovic much thought or any thought, in fact, after that, after I saw them there, met them, and I just wasn't really interested in them. I don't want to keep repeating the same things, but I was interested in finding out and meeting people who had some influence over the TO staff. They weren't those people and I had no interest in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you recall where precisely in Korenica you saw Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I saw him at Korenica hotel. Now, I really can't tell you when that was, but I'm 82 [as interpreted] and to recollect what happened 20 years ago is not easy, you can understand that, especially as it didn't seem very relevant to me, so it's very hard to recall the exact date or place or time of day when something happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Of course. And we all do understand the difficulty of recalling these events so long ago. With that in mind, do you recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps it's not relevant, however, for the transcript to reflect correctly what this witness said, he said that he was 72 years old, not 82 years old.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did I say 72 or 82? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness is of advanced age. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And do you recall where it was in Knin that you saw Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: At Korenica hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You've just told us about that time, my question is what location in Knin?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: At the fort, at the fort. When I say at the fort in Knin, I mean the premises that we had at the fort. At the Knin fort.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Maksic, I'd now like to get your comments on a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter number 412 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: This is a letter dated 1 November, 1991, from the Republic of Serbia Ministry of Defence to the government of the Republic of Serbia. The subject line indicates that it's a report on providing assistance to Serbian districts in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And if we could focus on -- yeah, that's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, please take a look at the document on the screen before you. Are you able to recognise the stamp or letterhead in the upper left-hand corner of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And perhaps if we could just enlarge the top half of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And let us know if you would like us to enlarge it or move to any other portion.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Can I see the signature under this letter, please. I'm not familiar with this letter, this is the first time that I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: We'll move to the second page in just a moment but I just --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: It says Republika Srpska here. It did not have a Ministry of Defence on the 1st of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we zoom in on the -- just the stamp in the top left-hand corner or the letterhead in the top left-hand corner of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. Actually, move it a bit to the right in respect of where I'm sitting. Thank you. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Now, are you able to read what it says in the stamp in the upper left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Republic of Serbia, Ministry of Defence, to the government of the Republic of Serbia. This is the -- well, you've moved it again. This is the Ministry of Defence of Serbia. It was good previously. Zoom in on it a bit. That's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can I just ask you simply whether you recognise that letterhead or stamp of what you have read as the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I cannot because it keeps changing. Can they just keep it where it was when it was good on the screen. Can we have it as previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a hard copy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a nervous mouse will be replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If it would assist, I have a hard copy in B/C/S. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And just again starting with the letterhead or stamp at the upper left-hand corner of the first page?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: That is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you recognise that letterhead or stamp as belonging to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was misinterpreted for the witness to whom the stamp belongs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Ministry of Defence is sending to the government of Serbia a report about the rendering assistance to Serbian districts in Croatia. The 1st of November. And it is signed by Tomislav Simovic, the minister. Lieutenant-colonel general, or perhaps, no, it was somebody else who signed the document. It is Kuzmanovic, actually. The letterhead is okay. According to the rules of official correspondence in the former JNA, this -- that we complied with, this document has been processed in full compliance with such rules on such correspondence. But there's something else which is not quite clear here, the Ministry of Defence is addressing this to the government of the Republic of Serbia, in fact, it is okay. It is good. So by this document, they are requesting assistance from the government of the Republic of Serbia to the Serbian Krajina. It is just that on behalf of Simovic it is signed by his deputy. On the 2nd page there is a specification of the requirements --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Mackic, I apologise --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I was just going to interrupt you at that point and move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: But I'd first like to tender this as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P968, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P968 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And if perhaps the usher could recover the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam usher, you are invited to recover the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, I'd now like to ask you a few questions about a different but related topic. Are you familiar with an institution or entity that was known by the initials SDK in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the social accountancy service, the public revenue service.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the function of that service.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I'm not a financial expert myself or an economist, but I do know that it was through this SDK that all transactions, all payments and -- in and out were made of course through banks. Enterprises would give them monies from it for salaries, some beneficiaries of the budget would also be using it because it was the overarching financial institution through which all payment transactions were made and that was the case until the year 2000, I believe, until a new law was passed, to the best of my knowledge that is. Once the law was amended, I'm not sure when that was, but I do know that all payment transactions and all monies were transferred and transacted through them up to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And during the time that you were in the Krajina, did the SAO Krajina TO staff make use of the services of the SDK in Knin?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. We received money from the Ministry of Defence of Serbia through the public accountancy service or social accountancy service as it was called, and then we would further earmark those resources, distributing them to the different staffs in the territory of Krajina, Banja Luka, Kordun, and northern Dalmatia according to their numerical strengths and according to their actual requirements, according to their numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And other than the TO, do you know whether any other institutions or organisations of the SAO Krajina also made use of the SDK in Knin?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I can give you second-hand information about this. The main financier of the former, namely the former commander of the TO staff of Knin, when he became the chief financier of the service, he knew his counter-part, his colleague in the Ministry of the Interior of the Krajina, and they would complain to each other along the lines are you getting more money or is the TO or is the police, and this was the subject of their conversation. And they would get money there together. However, money was also obtained through commercial banks. Not only through this SDK. From the ministry it was only obtained through the SDK, to the best of my knowledge. That was what we received, but there were also many voluntary donations and people paying in monies into the giro accounts held with banks in the different municipalities so that these -- both these two source, these institutions were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, during your time in the Krajina, did you ever have the opportunity to see the signature of Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Where did you --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: This was the way he would sign. Actually, he would just sign his initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Where or on what documents did you see his signature?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I received two documents from him over three months, and not I personally but the staff did. I believe that one had to do about agreeing on the use of the Golubici training-ground. And the second one I'm not sure. It was about some less significant issues. Actually, he just initialled them. According to the rules of our official correspondence, the signature was invalid if it didn't have the full name and surname, and Martic actually -- or you could just use the initial of your first name and the full surname, but Martic only signed his initials always.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity to see the stamp of the SAO Krajina MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is a small round stamp and they stamp it at the top heading, and the signature is also stamped with it. Where actually the signature block should be, they just write out or type out the Ministry of the Interior of the SAO of Krajina and everything else which the signature block normally has, and then they stamp it with this round stamp where the signature is. However, as far as the document content is concerned, they did not process it in compliance with the standard military processing, putting the initials, who typed it, who it was addressed, to whom were the carbon copies sent, et cetera. That was not respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the clock. I don't actually know what time we started, so I don't know whether it's time for the break yet. I am moving to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are close to the time for the break, so if this would be a suitable moment, we'll take the break now. But before doing so, Mr. Bakrac, I'm also looking at you, my understanding on the basis of the previous evidence was that the witness had a reason to celebrate his 71st birthday some ten days ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. It was but I didn't actually celebrate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the reason why I did not say that you celebrated your birthday on the basis of the evidence but you had a reason to do so. We resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just very quickly just raise one issue just to put the Court on notice that on behalf of both teams, at some point today, we would like to apply to adjourn the cross-examination of the next two witnesses. So I thought I'd raise that now so Your Honours can factor that into the day and also in light of Wednesday afternoon's possible sitting arrangement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's rather late for, I don't know of course what the reasons are, but we'll later hear from you. But before we continue, P951 is an exhibit number which has been assigned twice by mistake. Now, in order not to renumber all of them, the -- let me just see. In order not to change everything, 65 ter 1373, which is the transcript of the 55th session of the Republika Srpska Assembly, which was one of the two that received P951, will now receive number P969. So therefore the transcript of the 55th session now has become P969. Mr. Farr, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we now please have 65 ter 1546 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: This is a letter dated 10 February, 1992, from Milan Martic to the minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And if we could, if possible, zoom in on the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, taking a look at the screen in front of you, do you recognise the stamp that appears on that page?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we now have the middle of the page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, are you able to recognise the signature at the end of this letter?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is Milan Martic's signature, MM.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And the same question with respect to the stamp at the bottom of the letter, do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we now have the first sentence of the letter, which refers to a Minister Zebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And can I just ask you, Mr. Maksic, take a moment to read the first sentence and then tell us if you know who Mr. Zebic was?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: "Commrade minister, please bring your influence to bear on Minister Zebic to discontinue the practice of paying monetary resources through the SDK to the TO of Krajina because the MUP of the Krajina is not financed out of those resources, and we have been informed that an order has been given for the payment of monetary resources in favour of the TO Krajina, although the peace plan of the United Nations provides for the disbanding of the TO with the Krajina militia remaining as the only vehicle of duties to protect peace and maintain law and order in the territory of the RSK" --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic. That's sufficient -- unless you'd like to continue, please continue?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: There is one important thing here which I referred to in my statement an hour ago or previously. Namely that the SDK, the public auditing service, was the vehicle through which monetary transactions were made, and here -- I should read the whole text in fact. "We should like to inform you that the SDK holds an amount of 380.000 [as interpreted] dinars. These resources were earlier deposited for the Territorial Defence but since the major part of the defence, namely of the defenders, were financed from the army budget, the remaining -- the above-mentioned resources have been lying idle for a long time." Now, this is important. Please bring your influence to bear for these resources to be transferred to the giro account of the minister of the interior of the RSK, number so and so, but -- so it is not true that they did not have their own account, that they did have their account although this is from 1992 when I was not there any longer, but they did have such an account already in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can I ask you first to tell us who Minister Zebic was, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Minister Zebic was either the minister of finance or the minister of the economy, one of the two. I think that he was the minister of finance of the Republic of Serbia. A member of the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender 65 ter 1546 as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P970, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P970 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Turning to another topic, at pages 1167 to 1168 of your Martic testimony, you discussed your attendance at several meetings or briefings of the 9th Corps of the JNA. You also said that Milan Martic attended some of those meetings. Specifically at page 1168 you said: "Milan Martic attended two or three meetings because these meetings had to do with the engagement of some of the units of the Ministry of the Interior." My question is, were operational details discussed at these meetings in your presence?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And do you recall which operations were discussed at the meetings at which Milan Martic was present?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I apologise. When you said operational issues, I actually understood it differently. I meant daily routine issues, and you actually asked me about operations in terms of armed operations, no, I was not present when discussions were about engaging forces in specific -- for specific operations, but when the general situation in the territory of the Krajina was on the agenda, we who did not have any decision-making powers would thereafter be excluded from the meeting. And the commander of the 9th Corps, Martic, and sometimes the commander of the TO, General Djujic, would remain; whereas, everybody else would actually have been made to leave the meeting. I didn't actually understand properly the expression that you used.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification. You've mentioned who would remain in the meetings. Other than yourself, who would be excluded from the meetings at that point?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Everybody, but the three, these three men. Those who were in command of the armed forces, of the armed formations outside -- apart from the 9th Corps on behalf of the JNA it would be Milan Martic with his police and Mr. Djujic with his TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you a few questions about the participation of paramilitary formations in the attack on Gospic. At page 1194 of your Martic testimony, you discussed the involvement of several paramilitary formations, including Arkan's Men, Giska's Men, Captain Dragan's Men in an attack. At the beginning of your testimony today, you clarified that that attack was on Gospic. My question is, how did you learn that Arkan's Men, Giska's Men, and Captain Dragan's Men were involved on the attack on Gospic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I was informed of this personally by General Kovacevic who was the chief of operations in training of the corps and otherwise a personal friend of mine, and apart from that given the fact that he was the one who planned these operations and also the commander of the military police of the 9th Corps, he also informed me of this. They actually were co-ordinating, they were also part of this attack. The 9th Corps participated in it with a number of tanks, I don't know how many exactly, with artillery battalion and some other units, paramilitary, those that you enumerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And what was the relationship between the JNA 9th Corps and these paramilitary units during the course of this attack?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: You see, earlier on under our constitution, volunteers were permitted to form volunteer units. However, this lay solely within the competence of the JNA to organise them and train them. Volunteers were all those individuals who had not been given a particular assignment either within the TO or the JNA units or the MUP. Any such individuals wishing to apply to be volunteers, they had to go through an organisation in -- charged with national defence. In this case, parties were the ones that formed these units and consequently they could only participate in these operations through co-ordinated action, through concerted action.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to briefly ask you about Seselj's visit to the Krajina that you referred to in your Martic testimony. At page 1195 of your Martic testimony, you were asked whether you saw Vojislav Seselj in the Krajina and you said that you had. When asked about the circumstances under which you saw him, you said: "He came to visit the TO staff. I don't know whether this was something that was planned, although probably not because he was not on contract. I don't know Seselj that well, we just chatted about the situation in Krajina in general, whereupon he insisted to be received by Milan Babic." Do you know approximately when it was that you saw Seselj in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Again I repeat, I have this problem with the dates. I think it was in late November or mid-November. The only thing I remember of the day is that there was a very strong gale, the Bora that made our stay out in the field very difficult. But let me go back to what you said earlier on. Seselj did not get there in order to visit the TO staff. I don't know why it was that Seselj came to Knin. However, he came to visit, among others, me in the TO staff. I had seen Seselj previously on one or two occasions in the Assembly of Serbia and once I saw him as the president of the municipality of Zemun because I was the president of the association of reserve officers of Yugoslavia, so I was applying for some funds so that's where our superficial acquaintance stemmed from. So he came to see me, we chatted, and he said that Babic had refused to see him. Afterwards I went to see Babic myself and asked him what the reason was for his refusal to receive Seselj. I asked him why should he fear talking to anyone? Some ten minutes later, five or ten minutes into our conversation, and we were seated in a hall, a conference hall just opposite his office where he normally scheduled meeting. There was Milan Tarbuk there who had also been appointed minister of defence. Milan Babic through his secretary sent word to Seselj that he was now prepared to see him. Seselj only had to cross the office building and went to see Babic. I don't know what they talked about. Babic never told me and I never asked him about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: How was Seselj dressed when you saw him on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: He was wearing a military uniform complete with the boots. The sort of uniform that was worn in the army prior to 1964. He had boots on, trousers and helmet. He looked like a circus person. In other words, he was wearing a military uniform. What sort of uniform it was, it doesn't matter really now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Turning to another topic, at page 1260 of your Martic testimony you said that prior to being deployed to the Krajina, you had been the commander of the 151st Regiment of the Belgrade Corps for four years and that you had also been commander of the 505th Brigade. My question is, do you know what tasks, assignments, or operations those two units had between 1991 and 1995? More specifically, to where they were deployed, if anywhere?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, the brigades were deployed in their barracks, or do you mean whether they were anywhere, sent anywhere to the front, is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That was my question.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: While I was in Knin, additional men were recruited into the two brigades and in the meantime another commander was appointed for the 505th. It's normally this brigade exists only in the form of a part of the command and then people are recruited as required, and it was subsequently deployed to the front line in Western Slavonia. Oh, I said two brigades, you said regiment and brigade. In the meantime while I was there, the regiment was transformed into a brigade and that's why I said two brigades. It was furnished with an additional battalion and that's how it became a brigade, complete with some units attached to the staff, and they were on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And do you know approximately when these two brigades left for Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. I got there on the 27th of January, 1992. I was removed on -- in -- on the 7th of December, 1991, from my position in Krajina and by that time they were already on the front line, so it may have been sometime in the months of May or June. I'm not sure of that though. But definitely 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And do you know when those two brigades returned to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Upon my retirement in 1993, they had not gone back yet. Later on I was no longer privy to what was going on in life in general, and I didn't know what became of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksic. Your Honour, I have no further questions on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Farr. Who will be first to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will. Could I say at this stage I think we indicated by e-mail that I would take two and a half hours and my learned friends for Simatovic the same. In fact, as it has turned out, having discussed it with my learned friends, I will only take up to one-half hours and with Your Honour's leave they will cover the bulk of the cross-examination, so they, if possible, will take the time that I was requesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say that from five hours in total we go back to four hours in total, cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I was simply saying that of the two and a half hours that I originally requested, I would like to, if at all possible, give the Simatovic team --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One hour of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would still be five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see whether we grant the full five hours. It all depends on how focused you are, how well organised you are, what the relevance of your questions are. Let's get started and see how it develops, but I do understand that you have swapped some of your time to the Simatovic Defence. Then, Mr. Maksic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash is counsel for Mr. Stanisic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Maksic.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to ask you about something you spoke about ten minutes ago, which was it is related to the operational meetings where, I think you said the commander of the 9th Corps, Martic, and sometimes the commander of the TO, General Djujic, would attend?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Let me just correct you. The name is Djujic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, is it possible, do you think this is possible that actually Babic would attend meetings and you did not find out about that attendance?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: It is possible, but I don't believe that this was the case. Whenever he had contacts with the commander of the 9th Corps, Babic would tell me about it. But it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You are aware, of course -- well, I say of course, but you are aware that Babic pleaded guilty to various crimes in front of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on e-court please, 65 ter 1877, which is the amendment to the Babic plea agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just want to ask you if you might wish to comment on what it was that -- or part of what Babic agreed he had done and was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: While I was there over the three months, Babic did not commit a single crime because he was with me on a daily basis. What happened later I don't know. As for your last question, I'm sorry, why did he?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I'm just going to read some paragraphs to you and ask you about them. I think we've got on the screen what I'm looking for. If you just wait a moment, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see the amendment to the joint motion for consideration for plea agreement on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mine is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least on one of my screens, I must admit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't know if you speak English or read English, do you, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: No. I know a word or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest following: The technicians are unable to fix it right away. If we would -- could you read it slowly from your own screen, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I've got a paper copy, so as long as everybody else is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a paper copy in both languages?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, only in English I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only in English. Madam Registrar -- if you would tell us which paragraphs you need, then we could ask Madam Registrar to print out the relevant pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 25 to 30 and 34 and that's it for the -- I beg your pardon, sorry, I am looking at the first plea agreement. It's actually paragraph 26 to 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are pages 8, 9, 10, and 11 in the B/C/S version, but I'm now referring to the 12 that it's -- I think 14 to 19 out of 20 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me check. Yes. One second. Yes, then we do not have the whole of 34. I would say if we start at 25 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I could manage without 34, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, e-court pages 15 up to and including 19 or even 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Would it be possible for a copy to be printed for the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: No, in English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why don't you look at your screen, isn't that easier for you? I have it on my screen and you can -- you know that you can switch from one version to another, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: On the e-court screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: We've got no signal indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's on your left. But on your own manipulable. In e-court you can import, you have direct access to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll manage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see whether the print-out for the witness is already available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we could, as Your Honour indicates, start with paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you will get a hard copy. Mr. Jordash will draw your attention to paragraphs, and he will start with paragraph 25. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Maksic, I want to just take you to paragraph 25 and ask you to confirm, if you can, certain details, and if you cannot, then please indicate you cannot.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Give me a moment to find it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And may I just indicate from the outset, as I --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I indicate from the outset that I'm not seeking in any way to accuse you of anything. Paragraph 25: "On the 29th of May, 1991, the SAO Krajina Assembly with Milan Babic's acquiescence appointed Milan Martic minister of the defence of the SAO Krajina." Was that something that you were aware of, that Babic had acquiesced with that decision?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I wasn't there on the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So that you are aware of what this precisely is, this is a plea agreement that Babic agreed to. Reading on: "On the same day, the Assembly passed a decision establishing special-purpose units of the Ministry of the Interior of the SAO Krajina under the name "milicija" Krajina, the Krajina militia, which were put under the authority of the minister of defence." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this. This is the first time I'm seeing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That was not something that Babic told you about then?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Reading on: "At this time, Milan Babic was aware that forces under the command of Milan Martic were engaged in attacks on Croat civilians. On the 27th of June, 1991, the Assembly reappointed Martic as minister of the interior of the SAO Krajina, a role he had not in fact given up while minister of defence." Do you know about that reappointment? Can you confirm the sentence?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Moving to -- go on, sorry, I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about paragraph 25. However, what I do know, and there were attempts to discuss it this in Serbia as well, as for the attempts whether they tried to do it this way or not, I don't know anything about it. The ministry of police or the ministry of "milicija" was supposed to be the ministry of army, and they were supposed to be the only armed force in Serbia, or rather in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. That's why both the "milicija" units and -- the police units and the TO units were subordinated to Martic. And they normally have very little in common other than the operation that they are supposed to discharge together because the army, of course, is there to depend and protect, whereas the police is there to safe-guard the safety of civilians, to maintain law and order, and possibly to counter-sabotage operations. And it was only the anti-aircraft defence and air force that were to be left solely within the competence of the army. In this way, the government joined three functions, or rather two functions, and this is an attempt for the Ministry of the Interior of SAO Krajina to have a TO subordinated to it, whereas Milan Babic as it says here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a second, Mr. Maksic. Mr. Jordash, you read to the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you read to the witness a part of a plea agreement which deals with formal appointments.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the witness answers your question, your questions were rather vague, did you know anything about that, well, it's not clear what exactly you are asking the witness what he knew, whether it was a formal appointment by the Assembly or whether they took up that function. These questions are not very clear. Now, the witness gives a lengthy answer in which he starts explaining what the various functions of the various branches of armed forces or police forces were. It could well be that you are interested in that. It was not your question. Now, either you are interested in it, and please try to get by focused questions get the relevant information you would like to present to the Chamber, or stop the witness and say that's not what I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You should really be more focused and more clear on what you want to know because the witness starts telling after he said I don't know nothing about paragraph 25, and then he starts a long story about functionality of certain branches of the armed forces. And again, if that's what you wanted to know, then your question was wrong. If that's not what you wanted to know, it's not right to let the witness just tell it all. Then please try to get him on track on matters you would like him to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Moving to paragraph 26, please, the first sentence there beginning: "In July 1991 Milan Babic signed order as minister of the defence of the SAO Krajina creating TO formations within the SAO Krajina and appointing commanders to these formations."

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to understand it. Did you know that in July 1991 Milan Babic was minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you know that he was in any way involved in creating TO formations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: July 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I didn't know anything about the SAO Krajina before my arrival there. I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you not learn about this after your arrival there from, for example, Mr. Babic himself?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, no. You see, let's analyse this. If in July of 1991 there existed a staff -- a TO staff of Krajina, why would he re-establish it in September? It's difficult for me to reconcile the two. In July of 1991 Babic signed an order for the forming of TO units and appointed commanders. If in July there existed a commander of the Krajina TO, why would the government issue a decision to set up such a staff in September if such a staff was already in existence. I don't know if I've made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just ask you a question. Could it have been that a staff was later on set up to deal with the TO units that Babic had already been responsible for organising in July 1991 as he appears to have indicated by his plea?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV MAKSIC
utterances.text: I need to go back to the question put by the Prosecutor initially. There did not exist a single TO staff in Krajina before the 1st of September, to all intents and purposes. Had it existed in July, there would have been no need to establish it in September, there did not exist a TO staff of Krajina. There existed municipal TO staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
